name: Benzphetamine

card.summary: Old-school prescription amphetamine-type appetite suppressant labelled for a few weeks of use in obesity; Schedule III and not a cosmetic drug.
card.note: Controlled substance; label warns of pulmonary hypertension risk with use beyond three months.

quick.overview:
Benzphetamine is a prescription appetite suppressant related to amphetamine. In the US it is approved only for short-term use alongside a reduced-calorie diet in people with obesity.

It is a controlled substance and is not approved for cosmetic weight loss.
quick.mechanism: It is thought to increase norepinephrine and dopamine release in the brain's feeding centers, reducing appetite, and is converted in the body to amphetamine-type metabolites.
quick.risks: Reported effects include raised heart rate and blood pressure, insomnia and restlessness. The label cites an association between long-term anorectic use and pulmonary hypertension and contraindicates use in pregnancy. It is Schedule III in the US.

lead: Benzphetamine (brand name Didrex, also spelled benzfetamine) is a prescription appetite suppressant. It is used to reduce hunger so that a person eating fewer calories can lose body fat, which in turn changes how the face and body look: a smaller waist, a slimmer face and more visible muscle definition. In the United States it is labelled as a short-term adjunct, a few weeks, to a calorie-restricted weight-reduction regimen for adults with a body mass index of 30 or higher who have not responded to diet and exercise alone.[1][2]

It belongs to the sympathomimetic amine class alongside phentermine, diethylpropion and phendimetrazine, the older anorectics approved only for short-term use.[3][4] It is described as a prodrug that the body converts into amphetamine and methamphetamine, and it is a Schedule III controlled substance in the US, which Wikipedia notes is unusual for an amphetamine-related drug.[2][5]

Benzphetamine is a medical drug, not a cosmetic product, and the label does not describe it for cosmetic weight reduction.[1][5] Within appearance and bodybuilding culture it appears mostly as one of the older fat-loss prescription stimulants, and it is also named on anti-doping prohibited-stimulant lists that circulate in training forums.[6]

angle.text: By blunting hunger, benzphetamine makes a calorie-restricted diet easier to follow for a few weeks, and the resulting fat loss is what changes appearance. It is a prescription drug for clinical obesity rather than a cosmetic aid.

infobox: Schedule III controlled substance, prescription only

paras: The US label indicates benzphetamine for the management of exogenous obesity as a short-term adjunct to caloric restriction in patients with a BMI of 30 kg/m2 or higher who have not responded to appropriate weight-reduction efforts.[1] Reviews group it with diethylpropion, phendimetrazine and phentermine as the sympathomimetic drugs approved only for short-term use, in contrast with newer medications approved for longer treatment.[3][4]

Grokipedia reports that the drug was approved in 1960 and that trials showed modest additional weight loss over placebo that plateaued after the early weeks as tolerance developed; that source is AI-generated and these figures were not checked against trial reports.[7]

Appetite suppressants are discussed as adjuncts to diet and physical activity, and a drug-insight review describes them as helpful adjuncts for selected patients aiming to achieve and maintain weight loss.[4] Any change in appearance from benzphetamine comes through that fat loss. The US label states the drug is intended for obesity management rather than cosmetic use.[1]

The label lists palpitations, tachycardia and elevated blood pressure among cardiovascular effects, along with central nervous system effects such as overstimulation, restlessness and insomnia.[1] It warns against combining benzphetamine with other anorectic agents, including over-the-counter and herbal products.[1]

The label cites a case-control study in which anorectic drugs used for longer than three months were associated with a 23-fold increase in the risk of pulmonary hypertension, a rare and often fatal condition.[1] Valvular heart disease has been reported with some other anorectics such as fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine; the label states that no such cases had been reported with benzphetamine.[1] The drug is contraindicated in pregnancy.[1] Contraindications also include advanced arteriosclerosis, symptomatic cardiovascular disease, hyperthyroidism, glaucoma, agitation, a history of drug misuse and recent monoamine oxidase inhibitor use.[5]

A review of obesity-drug safety notes that the safety record of obesity drugs has historically been poor, citing withdrawn drugs, and reviews the safety of benzphetamine among the currently available agents.[8] Wikipedia lists dependence liability as high.[5]

Benzphetamine is thought to act like other amphetamines by promoting release of norepinephrine and dopamine in the hypothalamic feeding centre, reducing appetite; its exact mechanism is not fully established.[5] Tolerance and tachyphylaxis to the appetite-suppressing effect are described for the class.[5]

Wikipedia gives an elimination half-life of about 4 to 6 hours and notes that the drug is highly protein-bound and converted in the body to dextroamphetamine and dextromethamphetamine.[5] Grokipedia gives a longer half-life, so published figures differ.[7] A 1987 human laboratory study examined the reinforcing and subjective effects of several anorectics, benzphetamine among them, in healthy volunteers.[9]

Grokipedia gives a US approval year of 1960.[7] Legal status varies: Schedule III in the US, Schedule I in Canada, Class C in the UK, prescription-only (Schedule 4) in Australia, Class F2 in Brazil, and restricted to authorised scientific use in Germany.[5] It is the parent compound of the related anorectic clobenzorex.[5]

Benzphetamine appears on World Anti-Doping Agency prohibited stimulant lists that T Nation members have posted in supplement and drug-testing threads, and a 2003 thread lists Didrex among several prescription drugs a poster described holding.[6][10]

Published human work includes a 1969 controlled trial comparing single and divided doses of benzphetamine hydrochloride for pharmacodynamic activity, and a 1987 controlled trial of its reinforcing and subjective effects in healthy volunteers.[9][11] Reviews of weight-loss pharmacotherapy summarise it as one of the short-term sympathomimetic options.[3][4] A 2025 Cureus editorial discusses a theoretical potential of benzphetamine in ADHD.[12] No studies found examining benzphetamine for facial appearance or cosmetic outcomes.

lore.intro: Benzphetamine is rarely the subject of looksmaxxing threads; in bodybuilding forums it turns up in lists of banned stimulants and in poster inventories of prescription drugs.[6][10]

claims.claim: Didrex is an older prescription option for dropping fat quickly
claims.believers: A 2003 T Nation poster listed Didrex among prescription drugs they held in connection with bodybuilding, reflecting its image as a fat-loss stimulant.[10]
claims.experts: The US label limits use to a few weeks as an adjunct to calorie restriction in obesity and warns of pulmonary hypertension risk with longer anorectic use.[1]
